The shared benchmark measures the resulting solver, whereas these controls
ask which ingredients account for its behaviour. We begin with weak
endpoints, test local schedules and correlations, then compare certified
collective modes with classical mode rounding. Structure, timing and
encoding controls finally test how specific the response is. Each study
retains its own seeds, budget and endpoint: improvements on these known
graphs do not replace the frozen benchmark or establish unseen transfer.


\subsection{Weak endpoints}

The weak-case diagnostics identify two distinct issues:
probabilities can polarize around a poor cut before the final penalty ramp,
and cut-inactive vertices can still affect balance. This motivates tests of
the path and its correlations rather than additional endpoint descent.

The two weak cases have similar median net size, seven, but different
constraint structure. \instance{finan512} has 74,752 vertices and nets, 596,992 pins,
maximum incidence degree 55 and one connected vertex component. \instance{thermal1}
has 82,654 vertices and nets, 574,458 pins and maximum degree 11. Its
largest component contains 82,406 vertices; the remaining 248 vertices
are incident only to singleton nets and do not affect the cut. These
statistics come directly from the incidence representation, without
clique expansion or a partition-dependent selection.

Table~\ref{tab:weak-endpoints} resolves the median rows of the main table
into their two seed pairs. On \instance{finan512}, the winning raw and selected
partitions coincide and receive no descent flips. Their native cuts,
1,004 and 1,064, are already fixed while the balance penalty is small.
Across the diverse batches, median mean vertex variance falls to
$3.57\times10^{-8}$ at update 5,376, before the final penalty ramp.
The late ramp mainly changes feasibility, rather than the large-scale
cut pattern (Fig.~\ref{fig:failure-profile}). The two winning states have
zero and 18 balance-ignoring native improving vertices, respectively;
every complete-QUBO vertex flip still costs at least 56. These observations
support early polarization and a final coordinate barrier, without
establishing that polarization causes the entire quality gap.

\instance{thermal1} needs a different interpretation. None of the 16 diverse
replicas in either guarded seed pair is feasible at the final checkpoint;
six of 16 frozen replicas are feasible in each pair. The raw winners have
cuts 3,233 and 3,444 and assign all 248 cut-inactive vertices to one block.
The post-descent winners are different diverse replicas: they require
107 and 190 improving complete-QUBO flips, including 107 and 116 vertex
flips, and yield cuts 2,374 and 2,430. Thus the median change from 3,338.5
to 2,402 is a change in the winning candidate as well as its endpoint,
not the improvement of one raw winner. Even the selected winners remain
far above strict KaHyPar. Native-cut decreases considered in this
diagnostic are never applied when they violate balance.

\subsection{Local controls}

\subsubsection{Frozen and guarded portfolios}

We freeze one 16-profile portfolio before evaluating six additional graphs.
The four policy-selection graphs are \instance{IBM01}, \instance{IBM15}, \instance{IBM06} and \instance{bcsstk29}. Held-out
graphs are \instance{IBM02}, \instance{IBM09}, \instance{IBM17}, \instance{2cubes\_sphere}, \instance{G2\_circuit} and
\instance{PGPgiantcompo}. Each method receives the same nearby starts for base seeds 3
and 4, 6,000 annealing updates and 144 cold updates. The primary endpoint is
raw feasible cut; disclosed one-bit QUBO descent is a separate endpoint.
KaHyPar partitions are used solely as references.

Against the previous diverse portfolio, the frozen portfolio reduces the
geometric mean of per-graph median raw-cut ratios to 0.9586, an improvement
of 4.14\%. Seven paired graph--seed comparisons improve and five regress
(Fig.~\ref{fig:transfer}). The worst median
regression is 22.97\% on \instance{IBM02}. Applying one negative-contrast/warm-hub rule
to every replica performs worse: its geometric-mean ratio is 1.2056 and
\instance{G2\_circuit} regresses by a factor of 3.42. Thus, even a locally interpretable
rule can fail to transfer. The portfolio reduces this sensitivity without
eliminating it.

\subsubsection{Annealing and probe controls}

\instance{thermal1} separates numerical accuracy from discrete feasibility. The
implicit-root residual is of order $10^{-12}$, while thresholded ordinary

neither precise root solving nor lower variance guarantees a high-quality
balanced partition. One trajectory also exhausts its 50,000-flip descent
budget with a nonzero auxiliary gap. Its state remains in the record and
is excluded from feasible quality scores.

Let $\mathbf{B}$ be the net-by-vertex incidence matrix and
$a_e=w_e/\max(1,\lfloor r_e^2/4\rfloor)$.
The implicit clique Laplacian is
$\mathbf{L}=\diag(\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf{a}\odot \mathbf{r}))-\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf T}\diag(\mathbf{a})\mathbf{B}$.
We diffuse four fixed random probes in the zero-mean subspace using
$\mathbf{V}\leftarrow\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{P}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{V}/M$, where $\mathbf{P}$ subtracts column means and
$M=2\max_i\sum_{e\ni i}a_e(r_e-1)$ (bounded below by 2).
The filter uses 512 updates and QR orthogonalization every 32.
These are smooth probes, not certified lowest eigenvectors.

envelope restores $C_v=0$ before the cold phase. Preprocessing time is

evaluation inexpensive but implies dense long-range Ising couplings;
quantum hardware connectivity and precision costs are not evaluated here.

\subsection{Pair correlations}

The balance-variance calculation at the beginning suggests retaining
vertex covariance. The following control changes the trial distribution
while keeping the original binary problem; its cost and failures delimit
what this additional variational freedom achieves.

To test covariance beyond independent vertex marginals, we replace vertex
factors by joint four-state pair distributions. Block-factor trial
distributions are a standard extension of the independent approximation\cite{si-wainwright2008,si-zhang2026};
the following controls test that extension for this cut-net energy.
All four assignments remain
available, and an odd vertex is a singleton. Auxiliary Gibbs blocks remain
factorized from vertex factors. The full binary QUBO and its original
variables are retained; no logical-group restriction, incumbent partition
or binary exchange move is used. Random factors are predetermined per
replica; local factors greedily pair available vertices sharing a net,
with random fallback. All methods retain the frozen catalytic profiles,
nearby original fields, seeds 11/12 and 6,144 updates.

For independent factors $g$ with occupancy $S_g$, the exact balance
expectation is
\begin{equation}
\E[(S-b)^2]=(\textstyle\sum_g\E S_g-b)^2+\sum_g\operatorname{Var}(S_g).
\end{equation}
Within-pair covariance also corrects the temporary quadratic pair cost.
At nonuniform temperatures, joint entropy uses
$T_iH_-(p_i)+T_jH_-(p_j)+\min(T_i,T_j)\operatorname{I}(x_i;x_j)$.
Here $H_-$ is binary negative entropy and $\operatorname{I}$ mutual information.
This equals the old per-spin entropy at independence and joint negative
entropy at uniform temperature. The monotone implicit root uses 40
iterations versus 24 in the independent control. The singleton limit
agrees with the original equations when clipping is inactive; weighted
QUBO expectations, covariance
corrections and entropy derivatives agree with independent enumeration
and automatic derivatives. Joint log weights span at most 80, whereas
the previous tilted vertex fields clip at 20. Factor preconditioning and
root iterations also differ, so this is a complete-solver comparison,
not an isolated covariance ablation.

The completed 384-trajectory comparison is in Table~\ref{tab:paired}.
Local pairs reduce selected \instance{IBM12} median cut by 4.48\%, \instance{finan512} by 0.84\%
and \instance{IBM04} by 0.07\%, but worsen \instance{thermal1} by 26.84\%. FEM time increases
2.89--4.28-fold. Random pairs remove all infeasible \instance{finan512} readouts in
32 trajectories, versus 13 for the independent control, but have worse
selected cut. Pair covariance can reduce balance variance without giving
better partitions. These are exploratory seen-graph tests, not further
held-out evidence for the frozen primary policy.

rematching at updates 4,096, 5,120 and 5,632 on the two weak graphs, with

expected balance/catalyst energy; the jumps are recorded. It is a

Partner choices never use an incumbent partition.

\subsection{Collective controls}

The weak-probe results motivate a sharper test: certified low-frequency
directions rather than a fixed number of diffusion steps. The experiments
below distinguish their dynamical effect from simply rounding the same
classical modes.

The accurately converged spectral construction differs from the earlier
512-step diffusion probes. The latter were not certified low-frequency
modes and gave poor partitions. Here the active Laplacian is resolved
by Lanczos iteration\cite{si-lanczos1950}; the main text defines the resulting QUBO terms.
The resolved-mode control contains 18 populations, 288 trajectories,
base seeds 15/16 and 12,144 updates. Every arm retains the same local
portfolio, original random fields, penalty schedule, stopping rule and
auxiliary-only conditional readout. KaHyPar and binary spectral partitions
are never supplied to the solver.

later and anneals from 8 to 0.35 over the first 70\%, then to 0.02.
The matched long control instead uses the ordinary exponential schedule.

it gives no exactly balanced raw output; the selected cut is 276.
Adding the fixed random null-support coupling gives raw cut 255 for both
seeds, with zero winning descent flips. The signed/hold combination

Useful directions still leave the allocation of catalytic strength and
time unresolved. These controls alter structural weighting, coupling
envelopes and local-temperature envelopes while retaining matched starts.
Their regressions show why separately helpful interventions cannot be
assumed to combine into a uniformly better method.

We test five matched 16-replica paths on six seen graphs, with seed 21,
12,000 annealing and 144 cold updates. All 480 trajectories run on the
A100; a completed 80-trajectory \instance{IBM02} run on the 4090 is retained only as
a diagnostic and excluded from this comparison. Independent audits
reconstruct every initial field, score every raw and selected binary state,
verify zero final catalyst coefficients and check one-bit minima.
No winning raw state requires a descent flip.

The control uses unscaled incidence modes with equal first-two,
first-three, all-four or inverse-eigenvalue weights. An orthogonal
Hadamard rotation changes the orientations selected by replicas while
preserving the four-dimensional span. A coherence control weights
auxiliary polarization using
\begin{equation}
\phi_e=\frac{\|\sum_{i\in e}\mathbf{v}_i\|^2-\sum_{i\in e}\|\mathbf{v}_i\|^2}
 {(r_e-1)\sum_{i\in e}\|\mathbf{v}_i\|^2},
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the row of four modes, and zero denominators give zero.
Multipliers $\exp(c\phi_e)$ use $c=0.5,1,1.5,2$ across replica groups,
with the total auxiliary coupling mass conserved. A heating control adds
the centered, standardized and clipped log leverage
$\ln\sum_\ell v_{i\ell}^2$ to the existing temporary spin-temperature
field. The combined control uses all three modifications. Coherence and
leverage depend on the subspace rather than its orthogonal basis.
Every modification vanishes at the final original-QUBO endpoint.

\subsection{Penalty control}

A fixed hardening schedule can be replaced by a classical feedback rule.
Every 128 updates, let $f_j$ be the fraction of replicas whose thresholded
original-vertex labels lie within the requested integer count bounds.
The provisional penalty follows
\begin{equation}
\bar\lambda_{j+1}=\operatorname{clip}
\left(\bar\lambda_j\exp[0.5(0.75-f_j)],0.01,\lambda_*\right),
\label{eq:penalty-feedback}
\end{equation}
where the last two arguments are the clipping bounds and
$\lambda_*=D_{\max}+1$. The effective penalty is the larger of this
feedback value and a prescribed floor. The floor rises exponentially from
0.01 to $\lambda_*$ between annealing fractions 0.85 and 0.95; the remaining
updates and 144 cold updates restore $\lambda_*$. Thus the terminal binary
QUBO and capacity bounds are unchanged. Feedback uses the current
classical trajectory readouts.
Because the floor also differs from the baseline's final-10\% ramp, these
controls do not isolate feedback from hardening time. A matched-floor
control is needed before assigning a causal gain to feedback alone.

All arms retain 48 replicas, seed 21, the same initial fields, sparse
operators and single-bit original-energy readout. Six policies on
\instance{IBM01} use complete 3,000-update anneals. Selected policies are
then checked with 12,000 updates: feedback at 1\%, and earlier hardening
with warmer cooling at 3\%. Warmer cooling reaches $T=0.4$ at fraction
0.65 before cooling to 0.02. The earlier fixed ramp spans 0.65--0.9. On \instance{IBM13}, the baseline
and feedback use 3,000 updates at both capacities. These shorter runs
complete their own annealing schedules; they are not prefixes or early
checkpoints of a 12,000-update trajectory. All 20 QUBO executions and 1,920
raw/selected states pass independent native-cut, capacity, energy and
reported one-bit-minimum checks.

\subsection{Single precision}

To test sensitivity to arithmetic precision, we repeat the \instance{IBM01}
search with single-precision vertex fields, interaction products and count
updates. TensorFloat-32 matrix multiplication is disabled. The primary
benchmark and preceding kernel-fusion control use double precision and
are reported separately. Exact integer cut and capacity checks are
unchanged.

Count roots, auxiliary responses, sparse products and collective fields
are checked against independent double-precision calculations.
The separate mode-construction control uses FP32 sparse Lanczos
actions\cite{si-lanczos1950},
followed by CPU-double projection, QR and small Rayleigh--Ritz analysis.
Where needed, a CPU-double LOBPCG correction\cite{si-knyazev2001} is charged to preprocessing;
GPU actions remain FP32. On \instance{IBM01}, both mode sets pass the
unchanged $10^{-5}$ residual and $10^{-8}$ orthogonality/balance limits.
Their charged construction times total 3.96\,s, including 0.39\,s CPU
correction. This single case does not establish mode-construction scaling.

Continuous root diagnostics use
$\max(10^{-4},16\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}n)$ in FP32, versus
$\max(10^{-7},10^{-11}n)$ in FP64; this accounts for reduction roundoff
rather than changing discrete feasibility. For the three complete
\instance{IBM01} QUBO precision controls, the largest GPU root residual is
$1.22\times10^{-4}$. All 288 raw/selected binary states pass independent
cut, capacity, encoded-energy and reported one-bit-minimum checks. A
separate three-run QUBO check also audits 288 states with newly
constructed FP32 modes. It gives the same winning cuts in this case.

\subsection{Mode construction}

The large \instance{parabolic\_fem} cost has two measured sources. A repeat
of the original single-thread mode construction needs 15,375 unscaled
and 13,974 normalized sparse products. Those products consume 341.31 and
486.48\,s within total construction times of 1249.03 and 1293.90\,s.
The remaining time is outside the instrumented products. These diagnostic
repeats run separately from the primary measurements and do not replace
the original 1466.81\,s charged preprocessing cost.

On A100, CUDA-event profiling of the 48-replica \instance{parabolic\_fem}
update measures 38.66\,ms at the initial fields and 38.52\,ms at a
constructed saturated field. Sparse/catalyst gradients take approximately
27.3\,ms; the 24-iteration balance solve takes 9.5--9.8\,ms. The measured
update cost is consistent with the 467.52\,s primary FEM loop. Four balance
iterations take about 3.3\,ms and closely reproduce the 24-iteration result
at these two diagnostic fields. This is not a convergence guarantee for
every intermediate state, so all primary quality runs retain 24 iterations.
The saturated field is constructed from a saved binary state; it is not
a saved continuous checkpoint.

For \instance{scircuit}, the original unscaled shifted-Lanczos construction
was stopped after 2776.60\,s without a completed mode set. A
component-deflated, Jacobi-preconditioned LOBPCG block
solve\cite{si-knyazev2001} on the same incidence operator took 163.77\,s on CPU; a further 11.37\,s of CuPy refinement on
A100 certified all four directions. CuPy\cite{si-okuta2017} supplies
the GPU array and sparse-linear-algebra backend; the original operator
residual, rather than solver termination alone, is the certificate. Independent full-operator residuals
are below $10^{-10}$; balance and orthogonality errors are below
$3\times10^{-11}$ and $6\times10^{-14}$. This alternative was specified
before evaluating partition quality on this instance. It supplies continuous
coefficient modes, never a binary partition. The charged time includes
the unsuccessful CPU attempt, CPU warm start, GPU refinement and separate
normalized construction. The warm refinement time is not a standalone
GPU construction time. A separate CuPy solve from random continuous
vectors takes 19.08\,s and independently reaches residuals below
$10^{-10}$. It is an acceleration diagnostic and does not replace the
primary charged timing.

A separate full-precision incidence-product comparison on
\instance{parabolic\_fem} compares sparse-product implementations. For 48 replicas,
Torch CSR takes 6.53\,ms forward and 6.67\,ms transposed; CuPy CSR takes
1.82\,ms in each direction. A CUDA warp kernel takes 1.73\,ms including
dense-input transposition, or 1.14\,ms with prepacked input. All outputs
agree with the Torch products to within $3.6\times10^{-15}$. The 16-replica
products show smaller gains. These measurements isolate sparse products;
the custom path is not substituted into the primary quality runs, and
no full-solver speedup is inferred.
